intro: Here shapes such as a circle, a rectangle and a triangle overlap, and each shape stands for a group of people (for example cricket players). The number in each part tells how many people are in exactly that part. You count the people in a group, in two groups at once, in one group only, and so on.

tips.title: One shape, one group
tips.body: First read which group each shape stands for. Then for each number, ask of every shape: is this number inside it or outside it? That tells you which groups those people belong to. A number counts only the people in its own part, not the whole shape.

tips.title: "Both" means the shared part, and the middle too
tips.body: People who are in both the circle and the rectangle sit in every part inside both shapes. That includes the middle part where all three shapes meet. In the picture: 5 + 10 = 15.
tips.caption: Both ○ and □: 5 + 10 = 15. Only ○: 9.

tips.title: "Only" means outside every other shape
tips.body: "Only coffee" is the part of the coffee shape that no other shape covers. A shape can have two such parts, one on each side of another shape: in Q12 the circle has 15 above the rectangle and 2 below it, so 15 + 2 = 17.

tips.title: "Total" means the whole shape
tips.body: For all the students who study English, add every number inside the English rectangle, including the parts it shares with other shapes: 9 + 8 + 5 + 7 = 29.

tips.title: "Not" leaves out just one shape
tips.body: Dancers who are not doctors: take the parts of the dancers' circle that are outside the doctors' rectangle. They may still be inside the third shape (swimmers): 9 + 7 = 16.

tips.title: Look closely at the lines
tips.body: A number drawn near a corner or a slanting line is easy to misread. Check which side of each line it is on before you add it. A part with no number has no people in it.
